blurb: How well do you know your cat idioms? One round per chapter of the book. Name the idiom from its picture and its meaning.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The undisputed height of excellence and style”?
qs.x: The Cat's Pajamas: The undisputed height of excellence and style. Picture the literal article and you've already missed the point: a cat does not wear pajamas, and would sooner shred them than be seen in them.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Equally the best, with a touch more swagger”?
qs.x: The Cat's Meow: Equally the best, with a touch more swagger. If the cat's pajamas was the decade's favorite compliment, the cat's meow was its slightly louder cousin: the same idea with the volume turned up.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: The Cat's Whiskers: Precision, finesse, and the very finest of all. The British, never to be out-superlatived, had their own version: the cat's whiskers.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Unbothered, in the know, and effortlessly hip”?
qs.x: Cool Cat: Unbothered, in the know, and effortlessly hip. Long before the cat was cool, the musicians were.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Catwalk: The narrow stage where only the poised survive. Before it belonged to fashion, the catwalk belonged to anyone who had to cross something terrifyingly narrow without falling off.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Deep contentment, smooth and well-tuned”?
qs.x: Purring Like a Kitten: Deep contentment, smooth and well-tuned. We say it of a well-tuned engine, a smoothly running plan, a person finally at ease: purring like a kitten.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Top Cat: The one at the top, and everyone knows it. Every group has one, and everyone in the group knows exactly who it is.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Rich, comfortable, and faintly insufferable”?
qs.x: Fat Cat: Rich, comfortable, and faintly insufferable. Not every cat compliment is entirely a compliment.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Catbird Seat: The position everyone else wishes they had. Here is the odd one out, the cat idiom with no cat in it at all.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The smile that outlasts its own cause”?
qs.x: Grin Like a Cheshire Cat: The smile that outlasts its own cause. To grin like a Cheshire cat is to wear a wide, fixed, knowing smile that gives nothing away and somehow says everything.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Cat That Got the Cream: Pleasure as pure as it is shameless. Some satisfaction is innocent, or nearly so.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Triumph with a tell-tale feather”?
qs.x: Cat That Ate the Canary: Triumph with a tell-tale feather. This is the cream's wicked cousin.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: A Cat May Look at a King
qs.x: Copycat: Imitation, the sincerest and most annoying flattery. The accusation arrives early in life, usually on a playground, usually shouted.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The barb wrapped in velvet”?
qs.x: Catty: The barb wrapped in velvet. There is a particular kind of unkindness that never raises its voice.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Catcall: The jeer that started in the cheap seats. Long before it meant anything rude on a street, a catcall was a sound made in a theater.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The impossible art of leading the unleadable”?
qs.x: Like Herding Cats: The impossible art of leading the unleadable. Every manager learns the phrase sooner or later, usually while staring at a project that has quietly come apart in six directions at once.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: A Cat May Look at a King
qs.x: Sweeten the Kitty: Raising the stakes to tempt a yes. To sweeten the kitty is to make an offer more tempting by adding something to it, usually money, usually at the exact moment the other side is wavering.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The great leveller is a steady gaze”?
o: A Cat May Look at a King
qs.x: A Cat May Look at a King: The great leveller is a steady gaze. It is one of the oldest sayings in the language, set down in print nearly five hundred years ago, and it has lost none of its quiet defiance.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: More Than One Way to Skin a Cat
qs.x: More Than One Way to Skin a Cat: The enemy of getting it done is the single plan. Let us deal with the obvious at once.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The thief who waits for the perfect moment”?
qs.x: Cat Burglar: The thief who waits for the perfect moment. The cat burglar is the aristocrat of thieves, and the name is a tribute to a skill set rather than a species.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: More Than One Way to Skin a Cat
qs.x: Cat's Cradle: A structure that holds only under tension. Two hands, a loop of string, and suddenly a whole architecture appears between your fingers.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The plan everyone loves until someone must do it”?
qs.x: Bell the Cat: The plan everyone loves until someone must do it. The mice held a meeting.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Cat on the Fence: Committed to nothing, ready for anything. To sit on the fence is to refuse, deliberately, to come down on either side, and the cat perched on an actual fence is the picture the phrase was built from.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Treading so softly you never arrive”?
o: More Than One Way to Skin a Cat
qs.x: Pussyfoot Around: Treading so softly you never arrive. To pussyfoot around is to tread with excessive, maddening caution, to circle a subject without ever landing on it, to approach a decision on tiptoe and then quietly back away.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: A Cat Has Nine Lives: Built to survive what should have finished it. No animal has been quite so thoroughly insured by folklore.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The knack of coming through unscathed”?
o: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof
qs.x: Land on Your Feet: The knack of coming through unscathed. Some people simply land on their feet.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Cat-Like Reflexes: Faster than thought, and quietly smug about it. It is one of the proudest things a person can claim and one of the easiest to disprove.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Recovery in small, expert doses”?
o: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof
qs.x: Cat Nap: Recovery in small, expert doses. The catnap is the most efficient sleep we know of, and we named it, accurately, after the world's leading authority.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof
qs.x: Cat-Footed: Sure of every step, on any ledge. To be cat-footed is to move with quiet, certain grace, to place each step so well that you never slip, never stumble, never make a sound you did not intend.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Restless, jumpy, and unable to settle”?
o: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof
qs.x: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof: Restless, jumpy, and unable to settle. There are days when you cannot sit still, when every surface seems faintly too hot to rest on and your nerves will not let you land anywhere for long.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: Let the Cat Out of the Bag
qs.x: When the Cat's Away: What gets done the moment nobody is watching. The full proverb finishes itself, and everyone knows the ending before you reach it.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The question worth the risk of asking”?
o: Let the Cat Out of the Bag
qs.x: Curiosity Killed the Cat: The question worth the risk of asking. It is the warning every nosy child eventually receives, delivered with a wagging finger.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: Let the Cat Out of the Bag
qs.x: Cat in the Bag: The deal you cannot see into. Long before anyone let a cat out of a bag, the trick was to keep it firmly in.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The secret that will not go back in”?
o: Let the Cat Out of the Bag
qs.x: Let the Cat Out of the Bag: The secret that will not go back in. And here is the other half of the swindle, turned into the most useful phrase we have for an accidental confession.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Cat Got Your Tongue?: The silence that says the most. It is the question aimed at sudden, suspicious silence.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Seeing clearly what the dark conceals”?
o: Let the Cat Out of the Bag
qs.x: Cat's Eye View: Seeing clearly what the dark conceals. To take a cat's-eye view is to see what the rest of us cannot, to look into the dark and the hidden and come back knowing.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: A Cat in Gloves (Catches No Mice)
Not a Cat's Chance in Hell
qs.x: Not a Cat's Chance in Hell: Odds so long they barely count as odds. When we want to say that something has no hope whatsoever, we reach, oddly, for an image of a cat in the underworld.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The margin too thin to see”?
o: A Cat in Gloves (Catches No Mice)
qs.x: By a Whisker: The margin too thin to see. To win by a whisker is to win by almost nothing at all, by a margin so fine it can barely be measured, the breadth of a single hair between triumph and defeat.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: Not a Cat's Chance in Hell
qs.x: Cat's Paw: The one who does the dirty work for someone else. To be made a cat's paw is to be used, flattered into doing someone else's dangerous or disgraceful work while they keep their own hands clean and pocket the reward.

qs.q: Which idiom means “When the sky simply gives up”?
o: A Cat in Gloves (Catches No Mice)
Not a Cat's Chance in Hell
qs.x: Raining Cats and Dogs: When the sky simply gives up. It is the phrase that arrives with the worst of the weather.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: Not a Cat's Chance in Hell
A Cat in Gloves (Catches No Mice)
qs.x: A Cat in Gloves (Catches No Mice): Too genteel to get the job done. Here is a proverb with claws of its own, a warning dressed as a charming image.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Waiting to see how it all comes down”?
o: Not a Cat's Chance in Hell
qs.x: Which Way the Cat Jumps: Waiting to see how it all comes down. Before committing to anything risky, the cautious operator likes to wait and see which way the cat jumps.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Catnip: The temptation no one bothers resisting. Offer a cat catnip and watch its dignity evaporate.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Allure worn lightly, and entirely on purpose”?
qs.x: Sex Kitten: Allure worn lightly, and entirely on purpose. Of all the cats in the language, this one arrived most recently and caused the most trouble.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Alley Cat: Streetwise, ownerless, answering to no one. The alley cat keeps no address and apologizes to no one.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The charmer who never means to stay”?
o: No Room to Swing a Cat
qs.x: Tomcat: The charmer who never means to stay. Somewhere in the eighteenth century the male cat acquired a name.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Wildcat: The untamed streak no comfort can civilize. Underneath the lap cat dozing by the radiator lives a small wildcat that has merely agreed, for now, to the arrangement.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Fury too magnificent to apologize for”?
qs.x: Hellcat: Fury too magnificent to apologize for. There is a kind of anger that stops being a fault and becomes a force of nature, and English keeps a cat for it.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: No Room to Swing a Cat
qs.x: No Room to Swing a Cat: Confinement, and the whip that wasn't a kitten. You picture it immediately, don't you?

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Stray Cat: The wanderer who answers to no address. A stray cat belongs to nobody, and that is either the saddest thing about it or the most enviable, depending entirely on who is doing the looking.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Who's she? Manners, and the meanest pronoun”?
qs.x: Cat's Mother: Who's she? Manners, and the meanest pronoun. There is a very particular British rebuke, delivered to children and the occasional careless adult, that lands the moment someone refers to a person present in the room as merely she.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Glamour Puss: All surface, and what a surface. A glamour puss is a creature of magnificent surface, devoted to its own beauty with a single-mindedness the rest of us can only admire or resent.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The gentle housecat, and the timid soul named after it”?
qs.x: Pussy: The gentle housecat, and the timid soul named after it. Strip away the centuries of slang and the word is simply an old, affectionate name for a cat.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Crazy Cat Lady: A slander we should all be so lucky to earn. The crazy cat lady is one of our least fair stereotypes, and one of the most revealing.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Hopelessly under the paw”?
qs.x: Pussy-Whipped: Hopelessly under the paw. It is a crude little phrase, and an old observation dressed in rough modern clothes.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Scaredy-Cat: Frightened of everything, and unbothered about admitting it. Scaredy-cat is the oldest insult on the playground, the one children reach for before they can spell either word, hurled at anyone unwilling to take the dare.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The marshmallow inside the menace”?
qs.x: Pussycat: The marshmallow inside the menace. He's a real pussycat, we say, and we never mean it about the timid.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Sourpuss: The face that fun forgot. Some people wear their bad mood on the front of their head, and for them we have the perfect word.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: Look What the Cat Dragged In
qs.x: Look What the Cat Dragged In: The unwelcome arrival, looking the worse for wear. The cat appears in the doorway with something in its mouth, and the whole room turns.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Cruelty disguised as patience”?
o: Look What the Cat Dragged In
qs.x: Cat and Mouse: Cruelty disguised as patience. Anyone who has watched a cat with a mouse it could kill at once, and pointedly doesn't, understands the phrase in their stomach before their head catches up.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: Look What the Cat Dragged In
qs.x: Catfight: The fight we pretend not to enjoy watching. Two cats who have decided to settle something do not rush it.

qs.q: Which idiom means “One arrival, and the orderly panic that follows”?
o: Look What the Cat Dragged In
qs.x: Cat Among the Pigeons: One arrival, and the orderly panic that follows. Picture the dovecote: rows of plump, complacent pigeons, sure of their world.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
o: Look What the Cat Dragged In
qs.x: Fight Like Cats and Dogs: The eternal feud, and why it never ends. Some enmities need no explaining, and this is the one we reach for first.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Sudden departure, undignified velocity”?
qs.x: Like a Scalded Cat: Sudden departure, undignified velocity. There is no exit quite like it.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Lion's Share: The biggest portion, taken as a right. The lion does not negotiate at the kill.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Courage worn as a birthright”?
qs.x: Lionhearted: Courage worn as a birthright. It is the rare compliment that names a whole animal.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Tiger by the Tail: The triumph you cannot safely let go of. It begins as a victory.

qs.q: Which idiom means “The focus that arrives just before the strike”?
qs.x: Eye of the Tiger: The focus that arrives just before the strike. Before the tiger moves, it goes still.

qs.q: Which idiom does this picture show?
qs.x: Paper Tiger: The threat that folds when pushed. From across the room it is magnificent — striped, snarling, fearsome.

qs.q: Which idiom means “Character, and the lie of the fresh start”?
qs.x: Leopard Can't Change Its Spots: Character, and the lie of the fresh start. Try, if you like, to imagine a leopard deciding to become something else — scrubbing at its rosettes, willing them to fade, hoping to step out one morning as a creature of plain and respectable beige.
